questions.q: Why does a /26 subnet fit the office's needs?
options: It only supports 2 devices, enough for the servers alone
It provides 62 usable addresses, comfortably covering roughly 50 devices with room to grow
It is required for every DHCP configuration
It provides exactly 254 usable addresses
questions.explain: A /26 subnet has 64 total addresses (62 usable), which comfortably covers roughly 50 devices with some headroom.

questions.q: Why do the office's local servers get static address reservations instead of relying on DHCP?
options: Static addresses are required by law
So the servers don't risk being reassigned a different address by the DHCP pool
DHCP cannot be used in any office network
Static addresses make a device invisible to the network
questions.explain: Reserving addresses outside the DHCP pool for servers ensures those addresses stay fixed and are never handed out to another device.

questions.q: What did the 'isolate' step of the methodology reveal in this scenario?
options: That the inventory system itself was down
That a ping to the VPN gateway succeeded, meaning the tunnel itself was healthy and the problem was further along the path
That DHCP was not assigning addresses
That the office had no internet connectivity at all
questions.explain: A successful ping to the VPN gateway confirmed the tunnel itself was working, narrowing the problem down to something past the tunnel.

questions.q: What was the actual root cause of the connectivity failure?
options: The VPN tunnel was down
A firewall rule allowed traffic to the checkout service's IP range but was never updated to also include the inventory system's range
The subnet was too small to support any devices
DNS was not resolving any names
questions.explain: The firewall's outbound rule only covered the checkout service's IP range; it was never updated when the inventory system was added, so its traffic was blocked.

questions.q: What is the key lesson in why 'the VPN is up' wasn't the whole picture?
options: A working VPN tunnel guarantees every device behind it is allowed through automatically
A tunnel being up only proves the tunnel itself works — a separate firewall rule in front of it can still block the traffic
VPNs and firewalls are the same control
The statement was false and the VPN was actually down
questions.explain: The VPN tunnel being up was true, but it's a separate, independent control from the firewall rule in front of it — one being fine doesn't guarantee the other is configured correctly.
